title: Runners Keep the Same Schedule All Year, Daylight or Not | Terra
summary: We analyzed 2.6 million nights and 7,457 runners across 83 cities. The extra hour barely reaches your sleep, and once it’s dark, runners in UK cities use up to…
body_markdown:
## We keep exercising in the dark


Across the year, sunrise and sunset move by hours, but the busy times for outdoor exercise barely move (Figure 2). When the clocks go back, sunset jumps an hour overnight, but evening workouts start only about 4 minutes earlier. People keep their time and go out in the dark instead.


Through 2025, sunset in Europe moved by five and a half hours, from about 21:30 in June to 16:05 in December, and half of all afternoon and evening outdoor sessions started before 18:10 in June and before 17:35 in December.


***Figure 2:** Activities throughout the year mostly don’t vary with sunlight, activities are anchored to busy life schedules instead and 9am is the most common exercise time in the morning. The red lines are sunrise (bottom) and sunset (top), with shading for how they vary across locations, and the dashed lines mark the two clock changes.*


## What we change is *where* we run


We compared each runner's runs in the dark with their own runs in daylight at the same clock hour, in every city where we had enough runners: 83 cities and 7,457 runners through 2025. In 19 of them, runners spend clearly less of their route in parks and other green spaces in the dark.


The eight biggest drops are all in the UK and Ireland: Belfast and Bournemouth (36% less green space on dark runs), Newcastle (35%), Nottingham (31%), Birmingham (30%), Southampton (29%), Sheffield (28%) and Glasgow (24%). In most cities near the equator and most US cities we saw no clear change. In five warm cities (Querétaro, Jakarta, San Juan, Puebla and Abu Dhabi), dark runs actually have more green space.


The maps (Figure 3) show where runners stop exercising after dark (in red), which alternative routes show up (in blue) and which remain in the dark (in green). In London, runners stop running in Richmond Park, Dulwich Park and Greenwich Park but keep running in Battersea Park and Hyde Park. In Paris, two thirds of the route through the Bois de Boulogne disappears in the dark, while the Bois de Vincennes stays busy.


In Dublin it's Marlay Park and Fairview Park, and in Manchester, Heaton Park and the playing fields around Hough End and Wythenshawe. In Austin, the parks along the eastern end of Lady Bird Lake empty out while the central lakeside trail stays busy. The interactive map below shows every city we looked at; hover over a city, or click it to enlarge its map.


This happens on dark mornings about as much as on dark evenings (6% and 8% less green space across the first 16 cities we checked).


## Why these parks?


We can't tell from the data alone, but the parks people drop have something in common. Several of them lock their gates at dusk: Heaton Park closes at dusk\[3\], Greenwich Park closes around 6pm in winter\[4\], and Marlay Park closes at 5pm from November to January \[5\]. Others, like the Bois de Boulogne, stay open but are very large and dark, Richmond Park is defined as the darkest place in London at night\[6\]. Meanwhile, Hyde Park and the central lakeside trail in Austin keep their runners.


**Before you head out in the dark:**


- **Check your park's closing time.** Once the clocks go back, many parks close before an after-work run.
- **Plan a lit route now** , rather than finding out on Monday that your usual loop is dark or locked.
- **Morning runners too:** dark mornings change routes as much as dark evenings.
